Rebalancing with new savings: how much cash closes an allocation gap?

Four graphics show buy-only contribution allocation, the cash threshold for a chosen mix and the drift that remains when new money is limited.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 3 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore allocation changes using new money and no sales

Interactive planning lab

Asset A share before the contribution65.00%
Asset A share after the buy-only allocation61.90%
Cash threshold to reach the mix without sales$8,333.34

Hypothetical two-bucket allocation arithmetic in CAD, not an asset-mix recommendation or a security order. The chosen target is restricted to 5–95% for this illustration. Prices and existing holdings stay fixed; all new money is allocated, with no sales. Desired A buying equals target share times the post-contribution total minus current A, capped between zero and available new money; the rest buys B. The cash threshold rounds up to cents, while allocations otherwise allow fractional values. No actual lot size, spread, trading fee, tax, contribution-room limit, return, risk score or price movement is calculated. An empty portfolio has no defined zero-contribution weight; positive new money can still be allocated in the chosen proportions. A target reference row is not a claim that the available contribution can achieve it.

The central idea

New contributions can move weights toward a chosen target without selling. Whether they reach it depends on the existing holdings, the target and the cash available.

01

Separate maintaining a chosen mix from selecting the right mix

Rebalancing asks how to bring holdings toward an existing allocation. It does not, by itself, decide which allocation fits a person’s goals, risk tolerance, liquidity needs or time horizon.

The SEC’s Investor.gov rebalancing explanation describes selling overweight holdings, buying underweight holdings and redirecting ongoing contributions as different approaches. It also notes that transaction fees and tax consequences can matter.

This guide isolates the new-contribution arithmetic with two abstract asset buckets. A and B are not named securities or recommended investments. The target is a user assumption, prices remain fixed, and no sale, tax, trading cost or return is calculated.

02

Compare current dollars with a target at the same new total

The starting values are CAD 65,000 in A and CAD 35,000 in B, totaling CAD 100,000. A therefore represents 65%. The chosen hypothetical target is 60% A and 40% B.

Adding CAD 5,000 raises the total to CAD 105,000. At that new total, an exact target reference would hold CAD 63,000 in A and CAD 42,000 in B. Existing A is already above CAD 63,000, so buying more A cannot close the gap.

The buy-only allocation puts all CAD 5,000 into B. Holdings become CAD 65,000 and CAD 40,000, and A’s share falls to about 61.90%. That improves alignment without fully restoring the 60% target. The target reference bar is not an executed trade.

03

Use the contribution once and avoid an implicit sale

The desired new purchase of A is target A share × total after contributing − current A value. The model caps that amount between zero and the available contribution. Any remaining new money buys B.

A negative desired amount does not turn into an automatic sale. Instead, A receives zero new money. If the desired amount exceeds all available cash, the entire contribution goes to A and B receives none.

Those limits keep existing holdings intact and ensure purchases sum to the contribution. When enough cash is available, the model can split it between both buckets to reach the target under its fixed-price, fractional-value assumptions.

04

Calculate the contribution threshold from the overweight holding

When A is overweight, adding only B reaches the target when current A ÷ (current total + new cash) = target A share. Solving gives new cash of current A divided by target share, less current total.

In the example, CAD 65,000 ÷ 60% − CAD 100,000 is CAD 8,333.333… . The displayed cash threshold rounds upward to CAD 8,333.34. This is total new cash from the starting snapshot: the entered CAD 5,000 is part of it, leaving CAD 3,333.34 beyond that contribution. Practical order sizes, spreads and minimum purchases can still prevent an exact real trade.

If B is overweight, the corresponding calculation uses current B and B’s target share. If the portfolio already matches, no corrective cash is needed. An empty portfolio has no defined starting weight; the tool says so, although positive new money can be allocated in the chosen proportions.

05

Read remaining drift without interpreting it as performance

The contribution curve changes only new cash while holding current values and target fixed. Its displayed range ends no higher than CAD 200,000, so a large required threshold may lie beyond the plotted range.

The matrix varies targets and contribution amounts. It reports absolute allocation gaps in percentage points, not investment returns. For example, 65% versus 60% is a five-percentage-point gap; that is a different calculation from a relative percentage change.

Actual markets move while contributions accumulate. Account restrictions, transaction costs, taxes and the suitability of the target require separate review. This illustration does not establish that buy-only rebalancing is preferable to selling, or that either bucket has a better future return. Use it to understand the cash constraint around an independently chosen plan.
